name: Edge Counting Formulas (max/min edges under constraints)
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai maximum/minimum kitne edges ho sakte hain given constraints (n vertices, k components, bipartite, regular of degree d, acyclic/forest) — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (40 me se 13 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: Identify the EXACT constraint type (simple/connected/bipartite/k-components/regular/forest) and match the corresponding formula directly.
'Maximum edges with k components' trick: concentrate almost all edges into ONE big component, leave rest as isolated vertices.
conceptsRequired: Edge-counting formula library (min/max connected, bipartite, k-components, regular)
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify exactly which structural constraint(s) apply.
2. Select and apply the matching formula (n-1 for min connected, C(n,2) for max simple, ⌊n²/4⌋ for bipartite, (n-k)(n-k+1)/2 for k components, etc.).
3. For regular-graph-degree questions, use the handshake lemma: Σdegrees = 2×edges, so edges = (n×d)/2 for a d-regular graph on n vertices.
variationsObserved: Graph defined via a custom adjacency rule (e.g., 'i~j iff gcd(i,j)>1') — first figure out the actual edge set/count from the rule, then apply structural reasoning.
Degree-sequence-given questions (some vertices degree p, some degree q, rest degree r) — apply handshake lemma directly: Σdegrees=2E.
commonTraps: Using the single-component max-edges formula when k>1 components are specified — must use the concentrated-component variant instead.

name: Connectivity Structural Properties (cut vertices, bridges, min-cut, vertex-removal effects)
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai articulation points/cut vertices ki count, ya bridge kya hai, ya vertex remove karne ke baad components kitne honge — ye is topic ka doosra bada pattern hai (40 me se 11 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: A cut vertex/bridge is NEVER part of any simple cycle — an edge/vertex inside a cycle always has an alternate path around it.

Removing a vertex from a graph with c components: resulting components can range from (c-1) [if v was isolated-ish] up to (c + deg(v) - 1) in the worst fragmenting case — reason concretely per graph, don't assume a fixed formula.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. For counting articulation points/bridges: check each vertex/edge individually — does removing it break some pair's connectivity? (Equivalently, is it part of NO cycle?)

2. For vertex-removal component-count bounds: think about v's role — is it a cut vertex (removal increases components) or not (removal doesn't disconnect anything, might even decrease trivially if v was isolated)?
3. For min-cut questions: identify the smallest set of edges whose removal disconnects the graph — often relates to the MINIMUM DEGREE vertex (removing all its incident edges isolates it).
variationsObserved: Vertex cover / independent set size relationships (complementary structures: min vertex cover + max independent set = n, for any graph).
Adding a new 'universal' vertex connected to all odd-degree vertices — reasoning about the resulting graph's degree parity (turns all degrees even, useful for Eulerian-circuit-related constructions).
commonTraps: Assuming EVERY edge/vertex removal disconnects a graph — only cut vertices/bridges (non-cycle members) do.

name: Spanning Tree Properties & Counting
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai kitne DISTINCT spanning trees exist (especially for K_n), ya MST uniqueness conditions, ya spanning tree ki weight/edge properties — ye spanning-tree-specific pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Cayley's formula: complete graph K_n has EXACTLY n^(n-2) distinct labeled spanning trees.
MST is unique if all edge weights distinct — OR the more precise cut-based condition (unique min-weight edge crossing every cut).
conceptsRequired: MST uniqueness conditions (cross-link to MST topic)
generalSolvingApproach: 1. For 'number of spanning trees of K_n' questions, apply Cayley's formula n^(n-2) directly.

2. For uniqueness-condition TRUE/FALSE claims, distinguish the SUFFICIENT condition (distinct weights) from the exact IFF condition (unique min-crossing-edge per cut) — both may be tested as separate claims.
3. For weight-parity or other spanning-tree-weight-property claims, reason via specific small counterexamples if a general proof isn't immediately obvious.
variationsObserved: 'Largest k such that every connected graph with n vertices and m edges has AT LEAST k spanning trees' — a lower-bound guarantee question, different from exact counting.
commonTraps: Applying Cayley's formula to a NON-complete graph — it only applies to K_n specifically.

name: Adjacency Matrix-Based Reasoning (powers, trace, structural encoding)
recognitionClueHinglish: Adjacency matrix A ke POWERS (A², A³) ya TRACE ke baare me poocha hai, ya matrix entries se koi structural property nikaalni hai — ye matrix-algebra pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: (A^k)[i][j] = number of WALKS (not necessarily simple paths — can repeat vertices/edges) of length k from i to j.
trace(A^3)/6 = number of triangles in the graph (each triangle counted 6 times, once per starting vertex × direction).
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify what's being asked: walk count between specific vertices (compute the relevant matrix power entry), or a global count (triangles via trace).
2. Apply the matrix-power-as-walk-count interpretation directly, or the trace(A³)/6 triangle formula.
3. For general property claims about adjacency matrices, verify against a small concrete example graph.
variationsObserved: Diameter-related matrix construction (graph on A^k-derived adjacency, asking about diameter relationships).
commonTraps: Confusing WALKS (can repeat vertices) with simple PATHS (no repeats) when interpreting matrix powers — A^k counts the former, not the latter.

name: Special Graph Structures (Eulerian, Hamiltonian, line graphs, subset-based constructions)
recognitionClueHinglish: Eulerian circuit, Hamiltonian cycle, LINE GRAPH, ya ek graph jiske vertices SETS/SUBSETS hain (aur edges intersection-based hain) — ye specialized-structure pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Eulerian circuit exists iff connected AND every vertex has EVEN degree — a clean, directly-checkable condition.
Hamiltonian cycle has NO simple degree-based iff condition — much harder in general, don't expect a formula shortcut.
Line graph L(G): vertices = edges of G, adjacent iff they share an endpoint in G.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. For Eulerian questions: just check the degree-parity condition directly.

2. For Hamiltonian questions: no shortcut formula — reason case-by-case or recall specific known results (e.g., complete graphs K_n for n≥3 always have Hamiltonian cycles, with (n-1)!/2 distinct ones).
3. For line-graph or subset-based graph constructions: carefully translate the custom adjacency rule into a concrete small example first, then generalize.
variationsObserved: Counting distinct Hamiltonian cycles in K_n: (n-1)!/2 (accounting for rotational and reflective symmetry).
Vertices = subsets of a set, edges = subsets intersecting in a specific way — translate to small n first.
commonTraps: Assuming a degree-based shortcut exists for Hamiltonian cycles the way it does for Eulerian circuits — it doesn't in general.

name: Basic Graph Representation (adjacency list/matrix construction)
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek graph diagram diya hai aur poocha hai uska adjacency list/matrix likho — pure representational/mechanical pattern.
whatShouldComeToMind: Adjacency matrix: n×n, entry (i,j)=1 if edge exists, symmetric for undirected graphs, 0 diagonal (no self-loops).
Adjacency list: for each vertex, list its directly connected neighbors.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. List all edges from the given diagram.
2. Construct the matrix or list directly, mechanically.
